title: Linear lower bound N = Omega(n) for collinear integer distance sets

problemStatement.formal: For n distinct collinear points x_1 < ... < x_n with all pairwise distances |x_i - x_j| integers, the diameter D = x_n - x_1 = sum_{i<n} (x_{i+1} - x_i) >= n - 1, since each consecutive gap is a positive integer; hence D = Omega(n).
problemStatement.plain: Erdos #100 asks whether n planar points with all integer pairwise distances must have diameter growing linearly in n. This sub-problem handles the collinear case: when the points lie on a line, the gaps between neighbors are positive integers, so the diameter is a sum of at least n-1 ones and is therefore at least n-1. The goal is to formalize this clean linear lower bound in Lean.
whyMatters: Establishes the conjectured Omega(n) diameter bound in the one regime where it is provable, clarifying why the non-collinear case is genuinely harder.
Provides a self-contained, fully verifiable (sorry-free) lemma grounding the parent OQ-01 gap analysis in the collinear special case.

proven: Guth-Katz (2015): >= cn/log n distinct distances for any planar n-point set, giving diam >= cn/log n for integer distance sets.
Anning-Erdos (1945): no infinite non-collinear integer distance set exists; collinear ones such as {0,...,n-1} are unbounded.
Elementary: on a line, integer pairwise distances force integer consecutive gaps, so the diameter sums n-1 positive integers to >= n-1.
open: The full planar conjecture diam = Omega(n) for non-collinear integer distance sets (Erdos #100), i.e. closing the log n gap.
Sharper collinear strengthenings, e.g. binomial-type diameter when the distances themselves must be distinct.
knownResults.goal: Formalize in Lean, sorry-free, that any collinear n-point set with all pairwise distances integers has diameter >= n - 1, i.e. Omega(n).
